content: The following studies provide insights into infant feeding practices and their impact on growth, nutrition, and health outcomes: 1. The introduction of solid foods and the type of food provided can significantly influence infant growth patterns, as discussed in a 1998 Pediatrics study. 2. Marriott et al. (2003) conducted a randomized controlled trial examining weaning practices in preterm infants, highlighting the importance of tailored feeding strategies for this population. 3. Perkin et al. (2018) analyzed data from a randomized clinical trial and found an association between the early introduction of solid foods and improved infant sleep patterns. 4. Another study by Perkin et al. (2016) explored the effects of introducing allergenic foods to breastfed infants, demonstrating potential benefits in reducing food allergies. 5. Skjerven et al. (2020) investigated the use of skin emollients and early complementary feeding to prevent atopic dermatitis in infants, emphasizing the role of early interventions in reducing allergic conditions. 6. Kreyberg et al. (2019) examined the use of nicotine products during pregnancy in Scandinavia, shedding light on maternal behaviors and their implications for infant health. 7. Rehbinder et al. (2018) assessed whether the amniotic fluid of women with uncomplicated term pregnancies is free of bacteria, contributing to the understanding of prenatal factors affecting infant health. 8. Sloan et al. (2008) found that early weaning is associated with increased weight gain in infancy, suggesting the need for careful timing of complementary feeding. 9. Sreedhara and Banapurmath (2014) studied the relationship between complementary feeding practices and the nutritional status of infants, emphasizing the importance of appropriate feeding methods. 10. Sun et al. (2018) explored the timing of solid food introduction and its impact on infant body mass index, providing evidence for the role of early feeding practices in weight management. 11. Shim et al. (2011) linked infant feeding practices to picky eating behaviors in preschool children, highlighting the long-term effects of early dietary habits. 12. Zhao et al. (2016) identified inappropriate feeding behaviors as a significant cause of malnutrition in children aged 6 to 36 months in Myanmar, underscoring the need for education on proper feeding practices. 13. Miliku et al. (2015) examined the relationship between breastfeeding and kidney function in school-aged children, demonstrating the long-term health benefits of breastfeeding. 14. The WHO Working Group (2002) discussed the growth of healthy infants in relation to the timing, type, and frequency of complementary foods, providing guidelines for optimal feeding practices. 15. Hua et al. (2017) investigated the relationship between infant feeding practices and immune markers, such as fecal eosinophil cationic protein and serum immunoglobulin E, offering insights into the development of allergic conditions. 16. Hollis et al. (2016) found that the age at which solid foods are introduced is associated with feeding difficulties in childhood, emphasizing the importance of timing in complementary feeding. 17. Heinig et al. (1993) compared the growth of breastfed and formula-fed infants in relation to the timing of complementary food introduction, highlighting differences in growth trajectories. 18. Vijayalakshmi et al. (2015) conducted a study on knowledge and attitudes regarding complementary feeding, identifying factors influencing the age of introduction and its effects on child growth. 19. Huh et al. (2011) found that the timing of solid food introduction is associated with the risk of obesity in preschool-aged children, emphasizing the importance of early dietary interventions. 20. Ahmad et al. (2018) studied complementary feeding practices and their impact on the nutritional status of children aged 6 to 23 months in Aceh, Indonesia, providing evidence for targeted nutritional programs. 21. Eaton-Evans and Dugdale (1987) examined the effects of feeding and social factors on diarrhea and vomiting in infants, highlighting the role of feeding practices in preventing gastrointestinal illnesses. 22. Barrera et al. (2016) found that the age at which solid foods are introduced is associated with child obesity at 6 years, providing evidence for the long-term impact of early feeding decisions. 23. Bielemann et al. (2018) explored early feeding practices and the consumption of ultra-processed foods at age 6, linking these factors to dietary patterns and health outcomes. 24. Bell et al. (2018) found that the duration of breastfeeding, rather than the timing of solid food introduction, reduces the risk of overweight and obesity in children aged 24 to 36 months. 25. Carneiro et al. (2015) studied the growth of infants attending nursing appointments in childcare settings, emphasizing the importance of monitoring growth in early childhood. 26. Abraham et al. (2012) linked infant feeding practices to eating patterns in the second year of life and weight status in the fourth year, highlighting the long-term effects of early dietary habits. 27. Asfaw et al. (2015) reported a high prevalence of undernutrition among children aged 6 to 59 months in Ethiopia, identifying associated factors such as feeding practices and socioeconomic status. 28. Baker et al. (2004) found that maternal pre-pregnancy BMI, breastfeeding duration, and timing of complementary food introduction are associated with infant weight gain, providing evidence for the role of maternal and infant factors in growth. 29. Caleyachetty et al. (2013) studied breastfeeding duration, age of starting solids, and their association with high BMI risk and adiposity in Indian children, emphasizing the importance of early feeding practices. 30. Davies-Adetugbo and Adetugbo (1997) examined the effect of early complementary feeding on the nutritional status of term infants in rural Nigeria, providing evidence for the benefits of exclusive breastfeeding. 31. Grote et al. (2011) analyzed data from a European cohort study, finding that the introduction of solid foods influences growth in the first two years of life in formula-fed children. 32. Joseph et al. (2011) found that early complementary feeding increases the risk of food sensitization in a birth cohort, highlighting the importance of timing in allergenic food introduction. 33. Johnson et al. (2014) used SITAR analysis to explore associations between infant feeding and weight gain patterns, providing insights into growth trajectories. 34. de Barse et al. 35. Durmuş et al. (2012) found that infant diet influences subcutaneous fat mass in early childhood, providing evidence for the role of nutrition in body composition. 36. Kalanda et al. (2015) reported that exclusive breastfeeding during the first six months is positively associated with length-for-age among infants in Malawi, highlighting the benefits of breastfeeding. 37. Jeana et al. (2017) found that breastfeeding and red meat intake are associated with iron status in weaning-age infants, emphasizing the importance of dietary diversity. 38. Gingras et al. These studies collectively underscore the critical role of infant feeding practices, including the timing and type of complementary foods, in shaping growth, nutritional status, and long-term health outcomes.
